A LITTLE CONTEXT GOES A LONG WAY

Imagination, with the workings shown.

Nextstop is an experimental transit sandbox. It uses an explainable scenario model to choose up to three upgrades from six Toronto bus corridors. Change the assumptions and explore a different result.

01

Start with real streets.

The baseline uses actual TTC route and stop geometry, including Lines 5 and 6, from the August 27, 2026 data snapshot. Proposals follow portions of those bus corridors.

02

Compare possibilities.

The model compares bus priority, BRT, light rail and underground metro against construction and operating budgets. It can recommend no new construction.

03

Understand the tradeoff.

More stops mean shorter walks but slower journeys. Higher frequency requires more vehicles. Metro can be faster, with a much larger construction bill.

What this first version can tell you

Routes and existing stop locations are sourced. Costs, speeds and ranking weights are explicit design assumptions, not calibrated predictions. The model is rule-based; no live language model is connected. Population density now uses Toronto’s 2021 neighbourhood census profiles. It is historical context, not a demand forecast. A separate explorer shows published regional origin–destination totals, without assigning them to proposed routes. Toronto ravine and environmentally significant area boundaries add an initial environmental screen. Ground profiles use sampled polygon averages from Toronto’s 2023 terrain data. Corridor-level demand, geology and full journey routing are not yet integrated. No ridership, traffic reduction or financial feasibility is claimed.

The details that matter

  • Metropolitan context: this release evaluates TTC corridors. GO service, regional buses and committed future projects need a combined future baseline before regional benefits can be estimated.
  • GDP and funding: regional GDP is economic context, not money available to spend. The sliders are hypothetical investment allowances.
  • Environment: following an existing road does not establish permission to build. Connection details show 2D overlap with Toronto’s historical July 2019 ravine file and March 2026 ESA file, plus a 50 m proximity search. This is not a construction footprint, legal setback or impact estimate. Toronto ravine/ESA coverage outside the city is unavailable. A separate December 2023 Greenbelt outer-boundary screen flags planning review; it does not identify land ownership or the applicable designation. National parks and flood hazards remain unscreened. These results do not change ranking or costs. No overlap does not establish clearance.
  • Terrain: connection profiles sample the average heights of containing terrain polygons every 100 m, including both endpoints. The source is a 2023 LiDAR-derived TIN with CGVD2013 heights. The 2.5 m source resolution is not a claim of accuracy. Bare-earth estimates are not road or railway grades; bridge decks, tunnel depth, geology and groundwater remain unknown. These profiles do not change ranking, speed or costs.
  • Costs: modelled guideway, stops, vehicles and depot allowances, with a corridor complexity factor. Acquisition, major utility conflicts, financing, inflation and actual bids remain unresolved.
  • Travel times: length ÷ assumed speed, plus intermediate stop dwell and half the service interval. Excludes walking, transfers, crowding and reliability. The existing-bus comparison assumes 18 km/h and a 10-minute interval.
  • Population: uses the profile’s weighted 25% sample estimates, not the 100% enumeration count. Density divides that estimate by full neighbourhood polygon area, including non-residential land. Corridor context weights these averages by overlap with an 800 m straight-line band. Areas outside Toronto are excluded; coverage is shown. No walking access, current population or riders are inferred.
  • Ranking: combines neighbourhood density context, listed connection opportunities, modelled time savings and stop coverage, with cost penalties. The density weight uses an illustrative scale of 6,000 people/km², capped at 1.5; this is not a rail-demand threshold. If census data is unavailable, source bus-stop count is the fallback. Actual trip demand remains unknown.
